articles.text: Red Flag Warning for East Bay Hills, Piedmont until Wednesday morning The Bay Area Air Qualit y Management Dist r ict (BAAQMD) announced Monday, September 7 that it was extending a “Spare the Air” alert for the Bay Area, including Piedmont, until today, Wednesday, September 9. It marks 23 consecutive days of Spare the Air alerts, a bleak record for the agency. When Spare the Air warnings are in effect, people are advised to limit their times outdoors, especially those with who are sensitive to air conditions. Additionally, the use of fireplaces, wood stoves, pellet stoves, outdoor fire pits or other wood-burning devices is prohibited. BAAQMD said that very hot temperatures inland mixed with vehicle emissions caused smog to accumulate in the beginning of the week. Additionally, several wildfires burning nearby added to unhealthy air conditions in the Bay Area. “The Labor Day weekend heat wave, combined with tailpipe exhaust and lingering wildfire smoke, is expected to cause unhealthy air quality in the region,” Jack Broadbent, the executive officer of the Air District, said in a statement. “Driving less can help reduce smog and heading indoors when smoke is present can help protect our health.” Three massive fires caused by lightning strikes in mid-August are nearing containment but continue to burn around the Bay Area. (See details on page 14.) The Air District pointed to some other fires in Northern California that might impact air quality in Piedmont as well. Most fires were caused by lightning last month. The Woodward Fire has burned over 4,800 acres in Point Reyes National Seashore in Marin County and was 95 percent contained as of press time. The August Complex fire in Mendocino National Forest in Mendocino County has burned over 356,000 acres and is only 24 percent contained. This week, the National Weather Service issued a Red Flag Warning for parts of the Oakland Hills, including some portions within Piedmont. The Red Flag Warning, which indicates a high fire risk, was issued from Monday, September 7 at 10 p.m. to 8 a.m. today, Wednesday, September 9. Fire Chief Bret Black urges residents to create two emergency preparedness kits – a Go Bag and an Emergency Stay Kit. A Go Bag is a portable bag of items that should be prepared ahead of time in case an immediate evacuation is ordered. Information on creating a Go Bag can be found at ready.gov/kit An Emergency Stay Kit is a collection of gear in case a natural disaster, like an earthquake, limits mobility and requires residents to survive on what is at hand. More information can be found at resilience.abag.ca.gov/ preparedness/kit/ For more information, contact the Fire Department at 420-3030.
articles.title: Air District declares record 23-day Spare the Air alert in Piedmont

articles.text: Editor: Running for City Council in Piedmont is no small undertaking. It requires dedication, responsibility, and most of all commitment: • A commitment to community service. • A commitment to listen to Piedmonters’ input on the issues that are the most important to them. • A commitment to transparency and accountability for the decisions made by the City Council that greatly impact the quality of life and safety of the town we all love. • A commitment to be polite and courteous, even to those constituents with whom you might disagree. We have known Conna McCarthy for about 15 years and have been consistently impressed with her deep commitment to community service and her willingness to work hard on behalf of everyone in Piedmont. As the owners of one of Piedmont’s most visible businesses, it’s important to us that the City Council is made up of dedicated volunteers who will put public service ahead of politics and ensure everyone in our community has a voice in important decisions. We’ve both done our fair share of volunteering, parcel-tax wrangling, and event chairing in Piedmont. Every single time we were involved in a city-wide effort, Conna was with us in the trenches, working to ensure our city and our schools thrived. She’s been a part of each and every initiative that makes Piedmont so special, from Tri-School fundraisers to the Piedmont Educational Foundation to securing pickleball in our town. We believe in Conna’s intelligence, empathy, humility and work ethic, and we urge you to vote for her to join our City Council on November 3rd. –Laura Pochop & Chad Olcott “Don’t think of it as the minimum wage...think of it as a great career in the horse manure industry.”

articles.text: Editor: As a mother of two young children, my family’s journey within the Piedmont public school system began during a tumultuous time in our country and in our community. My mind has been spinning around issues such as school, racial justice, mental and physical health, social distance, breathable air. What next? And then I think of Veronica Anderson Thigpen, and her run for Piedmont School Board, and I feel reassured. Beyond her qualifications for this key leadership role in our community, she’s also a wonderful person who is giving and thoughtful with her knowledge and her time. She’s had a very personal impact on me and how I see and understand the importance of social justice and equity in Piedmont and the world. Veronica is someone that I can introduce to my children as a leader to be proud of, who represents every voice in our community. She brings a fresh perspective on how our school system can support our children and lift their voices. My family has been in Piedmont for four generations. I’ll be voting for Veronica for School Board to help guide Piedmont through the challenges our schools face in the years ahead. –Amy Whalen Griffith

articles.text: Editor: I am writing to encourage my fellow Piedmont citizens to vote for Hilary Cooper for the Piedmont School Board. I was delighted to learn that Hilary is running for the School Board. I believe she is just the type of leader who can help our schools navigate through these challenging times. articles.text: Editor Now is the time for the City of Piedmont to build a new swimming pool complex. That the existing pool is beyond repair is indisputable. It has given us many years of service, fully justifying the expense incurred from the time of construction to the last dollar spent on maintenance and repair. The need for Piedmont to have a swimming pool was clear 50 years ago. That is true even more now. Recreational swimming is one of the few forms of exercise that can be done throughout life. Competitive swimming is more popular than ever. Both are in jeopardy in Piedmont. Economics favor doing the pool now. Piedmont’s bonding capacity could not be stronger. Interest rates are at historic lows. Piedmont’s leaders are unanimous in wanting to go forward now. The stars may not soon again line up so clearly. Piedmont’s realtors are telling us the availability of recreational and competitive swimming is important for our property values. I can personally attest to that fact. My mother Jean Brown Wolfe’s parents built a home in Piedmont in 1921, and she attended Piedmont schools from 2nd grade through graduation from Piedmont High. She and my dad would have loved to raise their children in Piedmont but for one major problem: Both my middle brother and I were competitive swimmers, and there was no community or high school pool in Piedmont during the 50’s. Oakland High did have such a pool. That was one of the major reasons they bought a home in the Crocker Highlands area of Oakland and did not move back to Piedmont until we graduated. Piedmont should never again be without a pool. It is fortuitous that the bond measure to authorize construction of a pool is labeled Measure UU. Our leaders have done their part in putting Measure UU on the ballot. articles.text: Club Day to take place this week on Thursday and Friday All publicly elected officials and people in positions of leadership have been under a microscope of scrutiny this year, and ASB council members at PHS are no exception. They are not holding back right now,” said Edel. Davies echoed the sentiment that school has returned full force. “I didn’t realize that the teachers were going to use the whole 75 minutes [each period] – up to the last minute. articles.text: On August 2nd, American astronauts Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley returned from the International Space Station with a splashdown. Splashdown is a water-based landing in which a reentry capsule lands in a large body of water, often the ocean. The astronauts inside are brought to shore and safely returned home. Splashdown landings were used in the return of the Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo capsules. More recently, the SpaceX capsule, Crew Dragon, was added to the list as it successfully completed its first crewed landing in the Gulf of Mexico in early August, 2020. This marked history as astronauts Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley became the first astronauts to launch and land on American soil in over nine years due to the retirement of the Space Shuttle program. This mission’s purpose was to serve as a test-run and has already revealed ways to improve the design for the next launch. Now, we’re challenging you at home to design your own model capsule to survive the challenges of splashdown and protect the astronauts inside. CRITERIA • The capsule must stay together during landing. • The capsule must be able to float on the water’s surface for one full minute after landing. • Two astronauts must be secured inside of the capsule at all times. • The astronauts must be kept dry throughout the landing and floating period. MATERIALS Bucket, bin, sink, or tub Two objects to represent astronauts Containers or cups Coffee filters Pipe cleaners Popsicle sticks Glue or tape Markers Balloons Rubber bands Bubble wrap Foil Foam Cardboard Scissors Water ACTIVITY 1. Gather your materials. 2. Get thinking with some questions: a. How do you think astronauts return to Earth from space? b. How do you think astronauts are kept safe during return? c. What do you think are some of the challenges (or benefits) of landing astronauts in the ocean on their return? 3. Set up your “splashdown” site. a. This can be a bowl, bucket, sink, or tub filled with water. This represents the Photo courtesy of NASA/Bill Ingalls Crew Dragon capsule splashdown on August 2nd. Photo courtesy of NASA/Bill Ingalls Support teams arrive at the SpaceX Crew Dragon shortly after it landed. ocean that the astronauts will be landing in during their return to earth. 4. Select two objects to represent astronauts. a. Anything with a little weight – washers, figurines, toys, coins, etc. 5. Explain the design challenge and review the criteria (above). 6. 7. Design and build the capsule. Once it’s ready, test the capsule in splashdown! a. Hold your capsule high above the splashdown site. b. Give a countdown and drop it into the water! c. Determine whether the capsule survived impact by staying intact. d. If so, wait 60 seconds to determine whether your capsule can float. e. After, remove it from the water and check if the astronauts stayed dry. 8. Discuss the results of your first round of capsule testing: a. What did you try in your design? b. What did you notice happen during landing? c. What worked well and what could be improved? d. What else would you like to try in the next round? 9. Re-design and re-build the capsule with improvements. a. If the capsule did not survive, start over, using what you can. b. If it did survive, how can you improve the current design? 10. Once it’s ready, test the capsule again using steps 7a-7e. 11. Discuss the results of your second round of capsule testing using questions 8a-8d. 12. Repeat this process as many times as desired or until you’ve met all criteria. Haley Thiltgen is a Science Educator at Chabot Space & Science Center, 10000 Skyline Blvd., Oakland. It is a center for science learning featuring interactive exhibits, planetariums, a large screen theater, hands-on activities and three powerful telescopes. For more information see: chabotspace.org.

articles.text: School started three weeks ago, and it has been quite intriguing. Online classes are working much better than I thought possible. I think one reason is because teachers had more time to prepare over the summer. I know that my friends are enjoying the distance learning now in place. We’re even able to do group projects, thanks to breakout groups. Seeing what the assignments are on Google Meets works so much better than Schoology conferences. I thought I would hate distance learning this fall, but I don’t – even though I’d rather be in school. There are some pros to distance learning. For instance, you don’t have to get out of bed at 7 in the morning (unless you wake up that early anyway). School starts at 8:50 or 10:15 a.m., so I could not be happier. Homework is now being given with more explanation, not just “go write an essay in two weeks.’’ The teachers try to engage us and ensure that we partake in the activities. Also, the schedule isn’t as complicated as last spring. We are advised where to go and what links to click to get to various places. But there are some flaws in the plan. As example, people with poor wi-fi reception can’t really pay attention to the class because they are too busy trying to hold the wi-fi router in place to get into class. Once there, they can’t move for the fear of losing the wi-fi connection. Another issue is that it’s only a matter of time before Schoology, the online learning system, overloads and shuts down. it’s already happened once and was a problem across the U.S. There must be a better way for students and teachers to get into the classroom without accessing Schoology. Maybe teachers could send out an email that contains the link to the classroom as backup for when Schoology fails. For the kids with bad wi-fi, either get a new router or happy trails – because it’s going to be a tough ride. Let’s talk about distractions Then there are all these home distractions the teachers can’t do much about (nor can the kids). Last Wednesday when the heat was pretty unbearable, I was on the computer taking my history class, the final class of the day. I noticed that the faucet in the bathroom had been going for about 20 minutes, so I thought that someone was taking a bath. But when I turned my chair around, I saw water coming through the doorway. Hmmm. It seems that my mother had decided to cool the house down by filling a bathtub with cold water, but completely forgot about it. My sister, mom and I got down on our hands and knees to scoop water off the bathroom floor with a bucket and a dustpan. The whole time my camera was off, so my classmates had no idea I was running around trying to stop my house from flooding. Now that everyone is home and usually on a call, the wi-fi can get bad and people can get on your nerves. The whole thing seems like a mess. My sister is in the room next to mine doing her classes. and it gets annoying every day. At some point you just feel like walking into a wall and forgetting everything. But then you remember that everyone is trying to do their best while stuck in a house. So we keep our game face on, thank the teachers for their hard work, thank our classmates, and keep pushing through. We have four months left of 2020, and only God knows what will happen. Maybe we will have a zombie apocalypse – maybe we will find out that unicorns exist. But for now, congrats on getting through the first three weeks of school. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time.

HILARY COOPER 1 – My priority will always be the students. Re-opening our schools safely and effectively is going to be the most significant challenge our district has ever faced. It is incumbent on all stakeholders to come together at this moment to find a solution. I am very aware of the anxiety and fear that constrain our decisions, but we must continue to move forward with action. If we can acknowledge that there may not be a perfect solution for quite some time, then we can work on finding a solution. Beyond that, I think that our children’s social and emotional well-being must be addressed because no child can learn when they are struggling with motivation or self-esteem. Our students are missing the personal interaction of being in the classroom with their peers and teachers -- most especially our young learners. It is imperative that we find a way back into the classroom. 2 – Returning to in-person learning is a priority of my campaign. Many schools in the state have already applied for a K-6 waiver and that could afford us the opportunity to learn from each other and implement best practices. It’s important to let science drive our decisions, and studies have suggested that children under the age of 16 are far less likely to spread COVID than adults, and that it is unlikely for someone to contract COVID from surfaces. As we learn more and develop guidelines to ensure the safe return of our students to the classroom, I support applying for a special waiver for our youngest students. I am also interested in exploring how we can provide COVID testing for our students and teachers. We should strive to secure funding for such a program. We need to create a safe environment and get our kids back in the classroom. JASON KELLEY 1 – I’m running to: • Protect the whole community – students, teachers, families, and all Piedmont residents – by opening schools safely when the time is right. Families need as much stability as possible to plan for work and child care. • Make sure there’s a welcoming place for every learner in Piedmont schools. I want to see every student nurtured and challenged, whatever their ability, background or trajectory after graduation. • Plan carefully for what education will look like in the years to come. Students learn best in the classroom and need to be with peers to thrive, but lessons we’ve learned this year – and continue to learn – should help us prepare students for colleges and careers that may increasingly rely on remote learning and working. 2 – To apply for waivers to open in-person learning for elementary grades, schools must demonstrate compliance with a broad set of criteria designed to maximize safety. Applications must also show administrations have consulted with all parent and labor groups at each school site for which an application is being submitted. I think that consultation should be underway and ongoing. The principles that would guide me in making decisions about return to in-person learning if I were elected to the school board are: 1. Safety – ensuring schools have the resources to comply with health regulations to protect students, families, educators and the whole Piedmont community, 2. Stability – finding ways to make transitions stable and lasting so families can plan for work and childcare, and 3. Consensus – engaging in ongoing consultations to ensure all parties are heard so that any waiver application can be supported by the broadest range of stakeholders possible. HARI TITAN 1 – My focus would be a safe return to educational excellence. The spring 2020 incarnation of distance learning was more “crisis learning”. The new distance learning is working much better, however I see many issues needing a follow-up. I would focus on the correct scientific evaluation of the new distance learning model and would fight against positive spin. My focus would be on measuring learning loss of distance learning compared to classroom instruction as well as the social and emotional impact on students. After we got placed on the Governor’s watchlist, I began focusing on alternatives, like outdoor spaces and using larger rooms to teach subjects that need it most. Piedmont epidemiologist, Dr. Steve Sydney proposed that we do a small pilot study so we can figure out if students will actually comply with social distancing and masking rules in the classroom. I would work towards these goals while maintaining parent choice between hybrid and distance learning models based on what works best for each household. 2 – The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) announced Wednesday, September 2nd that it will begin the process of accepting waivers for classroom instruction. Alameda County waiver applications will have to pass through the county education office, the county health department, and then the state health department. The waiver process is rigorous (see: covid-19.acgov.org/schools. page. Applicants must involve labor, parent, and community groups in the reopening process. The entire process is expected to take weeks. In contrast, the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) reports many applications processed, mostly from independent schools. As of September 4, a total of 332 elementary schools applied for waivers and all but 9 were approved. The CDPH approved 16 schools in Marin, 15 schools in Santa Clara, 10 schools in Contra Costa, and 5 schools in San Mateo. No school district in Alameda County has applied for CDPH approval. CORY SMEGAL, Incumbent My priorities are: 1) Maximizing safe learning environments, 2) Creating opportunities to improve mental health, and 3) Maintaining fiscal responsibility. I believe it is critical during this crisis to focus on both student learning and mental health. From an educational perspective, many changes have been made to our distance learning process this fall that have improved the experience for our students. There is a consistent schedule, clear assessments, and accountability. While all would agree that in-person learning is preferred, teachers and administrators are working extremely hard to maximize student learning during this time of physical distance. We must not lose sight of the fact that distance learning is very hard on students and teachers from a mental health perspective. We need to create opportunities for all members of our community to make safe in person connections. I’ve suggested opening Witter Field for controlled student activities, such as small club meetings and more. My final priority is to maintain fiscal responsibility during and after the pandemic. 2 – I have been consistent and public in my views that we must prioritize bringing our youngest learners back for some in-person instruction. To apply for a waiver for elementary schools, districts must provide information that will show the ability to open sites safely. PUSD will detail the many precautions it plans to have in place that will protect both students and staff. For example, all students, even our youngest ones, plus teachers and staff, will be required to wear masks at all times. Students will be split into two cohorts to facilitate social distancing in classrooms. Extra cleaning protocols and proactive symptom screening will be diligently enforced. These precautions and others will help PUSD open our tri-schools safely so that our youngest learners, who may have the most challenges with distance learning, can safely receive some in person instruction. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received.

articles.text: Back in 1776, only select people had the right to vote: white men age 21 and older who owned land. Today all U.S. citizens age 18 and older can vote. So many more people have the opportunity to vote now, compared to 1776. Casting a ballot should be encouraged because it is not only a legal right, but also a privilege that many people do not have worldwide. When people have the chance to be heard, they should take the opportunity and an active role in our nation’s democracy by voting. For many years women, people of color, those who lived in poverty, or those who were uneducated were forbidden to vote. People in our nation’s history devoted considerable time and effort to fight for the right to vote. In the mid-19th century, many courageous women fought for suffrage, often sacrificing their safety and freedom as they were threatened, beaten, or arrested. It was not until 1920 that women were finally allowed to vote, a right that was legally recognized and added as the 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. Yet, according to The Washington Post, about 100 million people who were eligible to vote in 2016 did not vote and “[r] oughly 43 percent of eligible voters didn’t bother filling out a ballot”. That is a lot of people who gave up their vote. Americans only get to vote every four years for President, a person who has enormous influence and power over the well-being of our nation. Since the President can impact a person’s everyday life, voting can help choose someone best fit for the country. If people who did not vote are dissatisfied with certain policies or political leaders, they should take an active role so that their vote could work toward securing positive changes. In the end, voting should be highly encouraged because our ancestors had to fight for the right for all Americans to cast their ballots on election days. We are very privileged to be able to vote. Adding our voices to our nation’s decisions is a privilege and duty, and all American citizens should be encouraged to vote. Eileen Liu is an eighth grade student at Piedmont Middle School.

articles.text: LWV to host Sept. 20 discussion with polling expert Amy Simon The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host an event on the credibility and mechanics of election polling with Amy Simon, a founding partner of Goodwin Simon Strategic Research. This free event will be live-streamed on the League’s YouTube channel from 4:00-5:00 p.m. on Sunday, September 20. With the November election close at hand, viewers will learn how polls are constructed, fielded, and analyzed, and will have a better understanding of how to interpret them. A founding partner at Goodwin Simon Strategic Research, a national public opinion research firm, Amy Simon brings more than three decades of political experience to her work as a pollster and communications strategist. She conducts public opinion research on a variety of public policy issues domestically and globally. She has special expertise in conducting innovative qualitative and quantitative research on socially controversial and emotionally complex issues, with particular attention to developing effective messaging that has yielded a winning record on ballot measure campaigns. Simon is one of the leading architects of the freedom-tomarry messaging that helped propel voters in Maine and Washington state to support allowing marriage for same-sex couples in the 2012 elections. She has also Polling expert Amy Simon helped craft winning strategies on abortion, marijuana, medical aid-in-dying, climate change, insurance reform, and medical malpractice. With support from the David and Lucile Packard Foundation, Amy and her frequent collaborator, Robert Perez of Wonder: Strategies for Good, co-wrote Heartwired: Human Behavior, Strategic Opinion Research and the Audacious Pursuit of Social Change, a strategy guide to share lessons learned from their decades of experience on the front lines of social change. Their new, integrated approaches to audience research, storytelling, and persuasive communication have supported historic wins. In the guide, they share stories, tools, and some secrets of success

articles.text: Primoz Roglic jumps to the top of classification Don’t look now; the favorite has made his way to the front. 30-year old Primoz Roglic of Slovenia was mentioned as the Vegas favorite in our Tour de France preview a couple of weeks ago. The Slovenian won Stage 4 to put himself in second place overall. Several days later, he was 2nd in the Stage 9 mountain course on September 6 to become the overall leader, proudly wearing the yellow jersey to the delight of his countrymen. After Stage 10 on September 8, Roglic holds a 21-second lead over 2019 champion Egan Bernal. In last week’s story, Frenchman Julian Alaphilippe held the yellow jersey after Stage 4. He since has fallen far behind to 41st with a 52-minute, 9-second deficit due to a time penalty he received for an illegal feed during Stage 5. Virtually out of it, he says that he did not expect to compete for the jersey this year. “I never expected to repeat what I did last year. Last year was an exceptional season and an exceptional Tour de France,” said Alaphilippe in a story with Cycling News. After Alaphilippe, England’s Adam Yates held the top spot over Roglic until Stage 9, when he relinquished 54 seconds and subsequently fell to No. 8 in classification. As mentioned last week, the mountains are proving to be the changing ground when it comes to advancing or falling behind in the General Classification (overall standings). On Stage 9, Roglic and stage winner Tadej Pogacar distanced themselves from Yates up the double-digit gradient ascent of the Col de Marie Blanque. articles.text: Staff Photos The Five Lakes Trail of Alpine Meadows in north Lake Tahoe provides a 1,100-foot climb to a group of alpine lakes. Figuring out how to hike recently is an ongoing battle with smoke still settling around California. Even when traveling outside of the Bay Area, frequently tracking the changes to air quality is important. Temperatures began to scorch the East Bay last weekend, but Lake Tahoe and the surrounding Tahoe National Forest provided a brief escape from triple-digit heat and poor air quality. Which ranged all the way to nearly 200 on the Air Quality Index. But at North Lake Tahoe the air was consistently clear – and clean. Our Sunday morning the AQI was 57, though this writer did not experience affects from the smoke. Here are some guidelines to hiking during fire season and COVID-19: • Track air quality the day prior and morning of your hike. • Consider multiple locations given that smoke travels. • Always bring a mask, COVID is ongoing. • Check specific park websites for limitations, restrictions, or closures. • No large groups. Park officials request no groups over four. Some back-country hikers will search hours to find a location like Five Lakes, but with an hour’s worth of walking, the trail brings you to one of the most picturesque day hikes in California. Alpine Meadows is principally a ski resort community just south of Squaw Valley along Bear Creek on Alpine Meadows Road. The Five Lakes Trail is a 4.95- mile hike in total but provides around 1,100 feet of elevation gain in Tahoe National Forest’s Granite Chief Wilderness. Although a brief trail, it’s a good location for acclimating at altitude. The hike started at an elevation of 6,450 feet and topped out at near 7,600 feet. The trail connects with the historic Pacific Crest Trail. The trail goes on the southern ends of the KT-22 and Squaw One of the five accessible lakes, this is among the three in which you can swim. In the back is Squaw Peak. mountain peaks. To your left will be views of the pine tree-covered mountains of Scott Peak and the mosaic of jagged rock cliff faces toward Ward Peak. But given its location – surrounded by resorts and tourist destinations of Truckee, Tahoe City, Kings Beach and other North Lake Tahoe destinations – this hike can be a traffic jam. We passed 105 other hikers on the way to the summit and another 51 on the way back down, an average of 32 people per mile. This means your mask, along with some patience, is of utmost importance. Long portions of the hike are less than six-feet wide, making you stepping aside for groups a certainty. I passed at least three groups with more than 10 people, and many families with children miserably making their way up the mountainside. Faster hikers may find themselves behind slower traffic without a clear pathway around. But at the summit, a group of five alpine lakes are waiting for you. Despite the foot traffic and patience required to reach them, you can easily find your own area on one of the three swimmable lakes. Three of them had people cooling off in the water. Finding all three lakes could be tricky for some. The largest lake is near the main trail. Hugging its eastern shore brings you to another interconnecting lake, This lake is more marshy and un-swimmable, but equally as picturesque. Pictured is the first lake upon your arrival to the summit. The hike takes you under a tramway toward the summit of KT-22 above Alpine Meadows. A view of Ward Peak on the right.

articles.text: Piedmont Recreation Department’s registration for the next session of fall programs opened up today, Wednesday, September 9 at 8:00 a.m. for residents. The classes begin on September 21 and will include some safe and fun in-person classes and sports. Most programs will be in three-week long camps in stable pods of 12 campers each, with social distancing and shared equipment only among pod members of each pod. Class registration is on an individual day-to-day enrollment, without participants being put into pods. Pick and play classes operate with strict social distancing under the county restrictions for “Outdoor Non-Contact Fitness” classes. Another option is to bring your own pod for Camp Games with Michael Murphy. All programs require mask wearing and temperature screenings. For more information call 420-3070, or see: www.apm.activecommunities.com/piedmontrecreation/Activity_Search. Current programs offered are: 3-Week Camps Soccer Camp Baseball Camp Art and Action Triple Threat Basketball Flag Football Multi-Sport Camp for Middle Schoolers Jr. Fencing Team Breakdancing and Grooves Dance Camp Camp Smart Start Plug and Play 1-Day Classes Move & Groove Yoga Teen Yoga Camp Games with Michael Murphy Qi Stretches (adults) Agility, Coordination & Fun Bike Fun Hip Hop Dance Another of the three alpine lakes. where you also can swim. Perhaps the most hidden lake is just east. Staying on its eastern shore takes you to an open ridgeline where you’ll find the green valley of Alpine Meadows below you. The first mile of the trek has ab elevation gain of 660 feet, 430 of which is in the initial half mile, followed by a quick gain of 200 feet up two switchbacks. pages.text: Wednesday, September 9, 2020 13 HIKING WITH JON Staff Photos The Five Lakes Trail of Alpine Meadows in north Lake Tahoe provides a 1,100-foot climb to a group of alpine lakes. Following Five Lakes trail at Alpine Meadows By Jonathan Comeaux Figuring out how to hike recently is an ongoing battle with smoke still settling around California. Even when traveling outside of the Bay Area, frequently tracking the changes to air quality is important. Temperatures began to scorch the East Bay last weekend, but Lake Tahoe and the surrounding Tahoe National Forest provided a brief escape from triple-digit heat and poor air quality. Which ranged all the way to nearly 200 on the Air Quality Index. But at North Lake Tahoe the air was consistently clear – and clean. Our Sunday morning the AQI was 57, though this writer did not experience affects from the smoke. Here are some guidelines to hiking during fire season and COVID-19: • Track air quality the day prior and morning of your hike. • Consider multiple locations given that smoke travels. • Always bring a mask, COVID is ongoing. • Check specific park websites for limitations, restrictions, or closures. • No large groups. Park officials request no groups over four. Some back-country hikers will search hours to find a location like Five Lakes, but with an hour’s worth of walking, the trail brings you to one of the most picturesque day hikes in California. Alpine Meadows is principally a ski resort community just south of Squaw Valley along Bear Creek on Alpine Meadows Road. The Five Lakes Trail is a 4.95- mile hike in total but provides around 1,100 feet of elevation gain in Tahoe National Forest’s Granite Chief Wilderness. Although a brief trail, it’s a good location for acclimating at altitude. The hike started at an elevation of 6,450 feet and topped out at near 7,600 feet. The trail connects with the historic Pacific Crest Trail. The trail goes on the southern ends of the KT-22 and Squaw One of the five accessible lakes, this is among the three in which you can swim. We passed 105 other hikers on the way to the summit and another 51 on the way back down, an average of 32 people per mile. This means your mask, along with some patience, is of utmost importance. articles.text: Big Basin Redwoods State Park in San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties confirmed on Friday, August 28 that many of the famous old-growth redwood trees throughout the park remain healthy. Further assessment must be done to determine the extent of damage to trees from the CZU Complex Fire. Park officials state that their most famous grove, the “Mother of the Forest” and “Father of the Forest” were impacted but “generally healthy.” “Based on its initial appearance, the Mother of the Forest and the Father of the Forest trees were both affected by the wildfires but remain generally healthy. The Auto Tree sustained moderate to extensive fire damage but remains standing. Old growth stands in the vicinity of the entrance road and lower campgrounds appear to have experienced a range of fire intensities, with the upper crowns of some trees burned while other trees remained unburned. Additional assessments still need to be done to understand the health of these trees,” according to the park’s press release. The Mother tree has a 70-foot circumference and height of 329 feet make it a frequent visit for tourists. Another tree of mention, the Auto Tree, stands with a hollowed out interior and is a famous photo op in the park. Big Basin is the oldest state park in California, dating back to 1902 and preserves some Redwood Trees that are more than 2,000 years old. The park protects 35,000 acres of redwoods in the Santa Cruz Mountains, including approximately 10,800 of old-growth Redwood Trees. The old growth trees itself are known to be resilient. The trees within Big Basin, in particular, have experienced burns before. Despite some trees losing its canopies, they will make a return in time. That’s what makes the trees in Big Basin vastly different than the third- and fourth-generation redwoods at Joaquin Miller and Redwood Regional here in the Oakland Hills. “Old-growth redwoods have Photo courtesy of San Mateo County Parks Twitter Big Basin Redwoods State Park officials wrote in an official statement that many of its old growth redwood trees are “generally healthy” in spite of the CZU Complex Fire. Photo courtesy of Associated Press. The Mother of the Forest, the park’s oldest tree, is still standing. Photo courtesy of Associated Press. Another of the older trees in the park, the Father of the Forest, is also confirmed to be intact. Photo courtesy of Associated Press. Gov. Newsom stands within the “Auto Tree”, visibly burned, but still upright. experienced fire many times over the centuries, as evidenced by fire scars and dendrochronology. Mature coast redwoods’ thick bark and unique chemical composition make them highly resistant to fires,” according to a Big Basin statement. The CZU Complex Fire remains at 43 percent containment with 85,218 acres burned. Due to the fires in San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties the following parks and campgrounds remain closed: Año Nuevo State Park, Bean Hollow State Beach, Butano, Pescadero, Pigeon Point Light Station State Historic Park, Pomponio, Portola Redwoods, San Gregorio, Big Basin Redwoods, Castle Rock, Henry Cowell Redwoods, Wilder Ranch. Other fires Although the CZU sizably less acreage than the LNU and SCU complexes, it has the least containment of the three with the LNU at 69 and SCU at 70 percent containment as of Tuesday afternoon. The LNU has 375,298 acres burned and ranks third largest wildfire in California history; the SCU containment has ravaged 390,157 acres, ranking second in state history. The LNU has destroyed 1,288 buildings. Cal Fire officials announced that at least 274 homes were razed in Napa County, 268 in Solano County, and 118 in Sonoma County. Photo courtesy of Associated Press. Governor Gavin Newsom visits Big Basin Redwoods Park to see the fire damage. The SCU has burned down 120 structures through five different counties: Santa Clara, Alameda, Contra Costa, San Joaquin, Merced, and Stanislaus. Although no historic structures were burned, fires reached the Lick Observatory on August 20—but have since been contained without damage to the observatory.

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre is presenting Romantics Anonymous online on Saturday, September 26 at 1 p.m. Directed by Emma Rice, the play is based on the film Les Emotifs Anonymes, written by Jean-Pierre Ameris and Philippe Blasband. Wise Children, Bristol Old Vic, and Plush Theatricals will produce Rice’s critically acclaimed musical adaption of Romantics Anonymous, performed at Bristol Old Vic and broadcast live, direct to homes. The play’s protagonist, Angélique, is a gifted chocolate maker crippled by social anxiety. Jean-René is the boss of a failing chocolate factory. Angélique is so timid, she faints when people look at her; Jean-René so awkward he relies on self-help tapes and is prone to embarrassing sweating. When Angélique takes a job in Jean-René’s struggling factory, a fragile love affair unfolds. Factory owner Jean-Rene is played by Dominic Marsh, and Angelique is played by Carly Bawden. The cast also includes Marc Antolin, Philip Cox, Joe Evans, Natasha Jayetileke, Joanna Riding, Lauren Samuels, and Gareth Snook. Lyrics are by Christopher Dimond, and music by Michael Kooman. Rep 7-Play season subscribers will get free access to Romantics Anonymous. Log in to your account to renew online or select the Rep 7-Play subscription package of your choice. You must subscribe to the Rep 7-Play package by 5 p.m. on September 23 to get free access to Romantics Anonymous. On September 25, you’ll receive an email from Ticket Co with your unique reference code for the live broadcast. If you subscribed to a 2021 Rep 7-Play package before September 2, you’ll receive an email from Berkeley Repertory Theatre asking if you’d like to see Romantics Anonymous.

articles.text: From a Yuja Wang-inspired “fashion show” to performances by Kay Stern and other top Bay Area musicians, the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco will host a virtual Telethon this Sunday, September 13 from 12-8 pm. The event will launch their 2020-21 season of concerts. Admission to the Virtual Telethon is free, with performers and presenters encouraging viewers to make donations throughout the day. The CMS of SF Virtual Telethon will be a day of entertainment and fun, featuring performances and presentations - all with a musical twist. A m o n g t h e p e r fo r m - ers are Queen Elizabeth and Tchaikovsky Competition laureate pianist Stephen Prutsman, actor and comedian Tom Lenk, SFCM cello professor Jean-Michel Fonteneau, San Francisco Opera concertmaster Kay Stern, as well as demonstrations in french cooking, high-end coffee making and much more. The day will be capped with a grand finale concert at 6 pm featuring the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco performing music of Mendelssohn, Bach, and Haydn, as well as a preview of its 2020-21 season. “People have been doing telethons to fundraise forever and we thought it would be a fun way to bring fundraising online, with a huge diversity of kinds of entertainment for people to tune in to,” said Telethon Chair MariThe Chamber Music Society of SF will perform a virtual concert this Sunday, September 13. Pictured are violinists Jory Fankuchen and Natasha Makhijani. ana Roytman Schiffner. “We are thrilled to bring so many different voices to the conversation of why music, and chamber music matter so much, and how we can all support to ensure that CMS of SF comes out of this challenging period even stronger.” HOW TO REGISTER Telethon: Sunday, September 13th from 12 - 8 pm. Register at: https://chambermusicsocietysf. org/events About CMSSF Founded in the spring of 2013, the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco was born out of a collective desire to perform the great chamber music repertoire. Dedicated to bringing these masterworks to diverse audiences, CMS of SF is passionate about concertizing in intimate settings, creating close connections between performers and listeners, and cultivating a relationship between music and audiences that extends far beyond the perimeter of the concert hall. Founding members Natasha Makhijani, Jory Fankuchen, Clio Tilton and Samsun van Loon came together through their mutual love of the late Beethoven String Quartets, forming a core to collaborate with beloved Bay Area musicians as guest artists. CMS of SF brings together Bay Area musicians of diverse musical experience. They can be heard performing with the San Francisco Symphony, San Francisco Opera, San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, Oakland Symphony, Magik Orchestra, as well as many other chamber ensembles, including early music, jazz, tango, and pop.

articles.text: Composer Kev Choice The San Francisco Symphony has launched its summer 2020 digital programming, to include “Currents”, a four-part series. The performances are curated and hosted by Oakland Symphony conductor Michael Morgan in collaboration with San Francisco Symphony musicians and guest artists from the Bay Area. The Currents video series and companion podcast series explores the intersections between classical music and Chinese, Jazz, Mexican, and Hip Hop musical cultures. A concert will be performed every two weeks, and will illuminate the connections and ways that cultures influence each other and evolve together. The third episode, “From Scratch,” will explore the threads of Oakland’s dynamic Hip Hop culture. “Oakland is a city unafraid to speak up and speak out, with residents who loudly and proudly claim it as their own. I’m one of them. Art and activism go hand in hand here, and drive this city’s culture,” Morgan said. Emcee and lyricist Aima The Dreamer and pianist and composter Kev Choice describe how the culture of Oakland has shaped the genre of Hip Hop, The episode also features a new song by both musicians. Choice also discusses how he has been influenced by Bach, Stevie Wonder, Rakim, and A Tribe Called Quest. You can watch the episode at https://www.sfsymphony.org/. articles.text: A scene from Alfonso Cuarón’s Roma. Movie review by Chris Honoré Roma – the title is taken from the name of the middle-class barrio in Mexico City where director-writer Alfonso Cuaron grew up. It is, in the most wonderful, understated way. a poetic tribute to the women who raised him. Of all his films – Y Tu Mama Tambien, Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, Children of Men and Gravity – this is his most personal. It is also shot in 65mm black and white. The time is the early 1970s. The film opens with sudsy water thrown across a kaleidoscope of tiles. As the camera pulls back we see the maid/nanny, Cleo (Yoritza Aparicio), walking away, down a corridor, carrying a bucket and broom. She cleans the house, washes the clothes, nurtures the children, and brings them their meals, The family she cares for is composed of a mother, Sofia (Marina de Tavira), a father, Antonio (Fernando Grediaga), a grandmother (Veronica Garcia) and four young children. For the first hour of the film Cuaron allows us to dwell on the minutiae of their daily lives, all told from the point of view of Cleo. It’s obvious that she is indigenous, her skin a deep latté brown, her hair deeply black, while the family is as white as Nordic Europeans. Her wide face and deeply black hair say that while she is a member of the family, she also resides on its periphery. She soothes the children at bedtime, wakes them in the morning, and as the children cling to her it is obvious their bond is profound. Even when Cleo discovers she is pregnant, her place in the family is unaffected. What is significant is that the father of the child, Fermin (Jorge Antonio Guerrero), an obsessed kung fu neophyte and a coward, upon learning that Cleo is pregnant, immediately abandons her. In a movie theater, she sits and waits for him to return with ice cream. The second male to leave her is Antonio, a hospital doctor, who says he is going on a business trip to Quebec. In reality, he takes his mistress to a resort on the coast. Sofia, growing ever distraught, maintains a lie to protect her own children who begin to sense their father’s prolonged absence means more than they’re being told. And so we, the audience, are drawn into the very ordinary experiences of this family. Days pass. Months pass. Cleo grows larger. Still Antonio does not return. Life goes on. Patience required to know this family proves worthwhile. At first I was a bit distracted by the repeated wide screen shots. I wanted to move closer to Cleo. Observe the look in her eyes, the set of her mouth, see her protective hand placed on her expanding stomach. Gradually the camera does move closer. The pace begins to accelerate and Cuaron engages us, culminating in several scenes that are heartbreaking and breathtaking in their stark loveliness. Later, there is a long wide angle shot of two of the children wading out in the ocean, going too far, suddenly in trouble, and Cleo, who cannot swim, walking deliberately through the waves, on the precipice of being overcome, unwavering in her attempt to rescue them. It’s a wrenchingly beautiful moment, the connection between her and the children touchingly inviolable. Roma repeatedly asks the question: what is the relationship between the moviegoer and the story? What are our expectations? To select a film, sit in a theater, which is where Roma should be seen (not on a small screen of any kind), is aspirational. We want to be pulled into a narrative that in some way touches us, that exists somewhere on the spectrum of emotions. Cuaron’s movie asks a great deal of us. Wait. Watch. Allow the vignettes – and Roma is constructed of a series of tightly crafted moments – to build, allow them to be slowly fitted together. And then relish the final scenes that are so wonderfully human, each a revelation. Nominated for seven Academy Awards, Roma and Cuaron walked away with an Oscar for Best International Feaature Film. Clearly it was embraced by the Academy of Motion Pictures in acknowledging the fine work of its director, Alfonso Cuaron Roma (2018). In Spanish with subtitles Written and directed by Alfonso Cuaron. 2 hrs., 15 min.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré It’s supremely difficult to make a good movie about adolescents. It’s the equivalent of trying to capture lightning in a bottle: years of emotional riptides, dramatic changes, layered with confusion and clarity and idealism. Which is why so many Hollywood teen movies seem shallow, trivial, and too often buried beneath an avalanche of stereotypes and clichés. Unexpectedly, It’s Kind of a Funny Story gets it just about right. It’s sweet and poignant, certainly relevant, and it’s aimed directly at young people who should instantly recognize the existential crisis of 16-year-old Craig (Keir Gilchrist) who is definitely one of their own. Craig, nudged by depression (he’s seeing a therapist, taking some Zoloft), feeling overwhelmed by the pressures of high school and the expectations of his parents, is stalked by thoughts of suicide. He heads toward the George Washington bridge in New York one morning, contemplating jumping. Instead he detours to Argeron Hospital, in Brooklyn, and, after a cryptic conversation with one of the Docs, unwittingly checks himself into the psych ward. Because the children’s ward is closed for renovations, he finds himself among the general population and quickly realizes – whoops! — perhaps it would be better if he just, like, went home. No harm, no foul. Plus, well, he’s got school the next day and a paper is due. He soon learns that he is there for a five-day evaluation. His parents, as it turns out, agree, and thus begins Craig’s very strange and enlightening odyssey. Writers and directors Ryan Fleck and Anna Boden walk a precarious line between the dark tragedies that define severe mental illness and the comedic and the light-hearted moments encountered by Craig as he navigates the ward. He is mentored, in a touching and heartfelt way, by Bobby (Zach Galifianakis), who has a wife and young daughter, and who not only has suicide ideation, but has tried to kill himself several times. And there’s Noelle (Emma Roberts), a love interest, who is hospitalized because she is a cutter. Craig is also gently guided and helped by the resident psychiatrist, Dr. Minerva (Viola Davis), who gives him increasing support and insight as he sorts out his feelings. While watching the relationship between Craig and Noelle grow, as they reach out to one another for understanding and tentative love, it begs an interesting question: can adolescents truly help one another through their long and often painful rite of passage? The answer is probably yes – and no. The fact is that turning to one another is the default response of most teenagers to the exigencies of growing up. Friends have an exalted status. Their counsel is weighted heavily. Adults, in contrast, have to tenaciously insert themselves into the lives of adolescents, no matter the reflexive resistance – which is what happens to Craig in a kind of wonderful way during his remarkable five days on the ward. It’s Kind of a Funny Story would be a great movie to see with a teenager, a son or daughter, hopefully resulting in a conversation post-screening. Know that the film strikes just the right note between the realities of teen suicide, and the ability of a young, intelligent kid to realize that the gestalt of emotions that seem so perplexing and contradictory can ultimately be understood and dealt with. It’s Kind of a Funny Story. Starring Keir Gilchrist, Emma Roberts, Zoe Kravitz, Zach Galifianakis and Viola Davis. Written and directed by Ryan Fleck and Anna Boden. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: It’s Kind of a Funny Story a charming tale for parents and teens

Though it’s billed as a film about a sweet, ever disobedient Golden Lab, it proves instead to be about a couple, Jenny (Jennifer Aniston) and John (Owen Wilson), who adopt an irresistible pup, Marley, and then, over the next 12 years, go on to have three children, transforming their lives. Marley is the sixth member of a family and though his antics often dominate, making for some comedic moments, he never overwhelms what turns out to be a nicely told movie about the messiness and compromises involved in having children and keeping everything and everyone afloat. Marley, as it turns out, represents nicely all those aspects of life that seem impossible to contain. Shirttails are always slightly un-tucked. Nothing is ever symmetrical. articles.text: During the dark days of life in a time of a worldwide pandemic due to coronavirus, some levity distinctly is in order. For fans of the English language, and those who can remember being taught the many parts of the language, here’s a little refresher, all based upon the well-worn joke, “A man walks into a bar….” • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • The past, present, and future walked into a bar. It was tense. An Oxford comma walks into a bar where it spends the evening watching the television getting drunk and smoking cigars. A dangling participle walks into a bar. Enjoying a cocktail and chatting with the bartender, the evening passes pleasantly. A bar was walked into by the passive voice. An oxymoron walked into a bar, and the silence was deafening. Two quotation marks walk into a “bar.” A malapropism walks into a bar, looking for all intensive purposes like a wolf in cheap clothing, muttering epitaphs and casting dispersions on his magnificent other, who takes him for granite. Hyperbole totally rips into this insane bar and absolutely destroys everything. A question mark walks into a bar? A non sequitur walks into a bar. In a strong wind, even turkeys can fly. Papyrus and Comic Sans walk into a bar. The bartender says, “Get out -- we don’t serve your type.” A mixed metaphor walks into a bar, seeing the handwriting on the wall but hoping to nip it in the bud. A comma splice walks into a bar, it has a drink and then leaves. Three intransitive verbs walk into a bar. They sit. They converse. They depart. A synonym strolls into a tavern. At the end of the day, a cliché walks into a bar -- fresh as a daisy, cute as a button, and sharp as a tack. A run-on sentence walks into a bar it starts flirting. With a cute little sentence fragment. Falling slowly, softly falling, the chiasmus collapses to the bar floor. A figure of speech literally walks into a bar and ends up getting figuratively hammered. An allusion walks into a bar, despite the fact that alcohol is its Achilles heel. The subjunctive would have walked into a bar, had it only known. A misplaced modifier walks into a bar owned by a man with a glass eye named Ralph. A dyslexic walks into a bra. A verb walks into a bar, sees a beautiful noun, and suggests they conjugate. The noun declines. A simile walks into a bar, as parched as a desert. A gerund and an infinitive walk into a bar, drinking to forget. A hyphenated word and a non-hyphenated word walk into a bar and the bartender nearly chokes on the irony.

Smaller shrubbery can provide screening between uses, a soft background to open space, or a foreground and transition to yet smaller plantings. This kind of detail is also valuable to the community because it exhibits care and ownership Different scales of planting. — clearly it takes someone to plan and continually maintain beautiful landscaping. There are many kinds of fences and gates possible: stone, masonry, iron, stucco, and wood of different designs and finishes. When someone uses a spiritual bypass to get through a difficult time in their lives or to deal with confrontation, they are looking for a quick fix. Spiritual bypass is about doing things that may feel good or make you happy in the short term, They include glossing over difficulties with affirmations or going on spiritual retreats, while skipping the hard work of looking at underlying systems of feeling the grief or pain that might be underneath the issues one is facing, all of which mean slowing down. Spiritual seekers and homeowners both can benefit from slowing down. articles.text: Alyssa Maldonado, Veterinarian Technician, performs an initial examination on one of the 20 Riparian Brush rabbits temporarily housed at Oakland Zoo Veterinary Hospital while undergoing vaccinations against the Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease Virus (RHDV2). Oakland Zoo’s focus on species conservation now includes an effort to help prevent the possible extinction of the Riparian Brush rabbit. The sub-species is threatened by Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease Virus (RHDV2); a European-borne virus that has spread to many species of wild rabbit populations across the United States. The Oakland Zoo has partnered with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, California Department of Fish and Wildlife, U.S. Geological Survey, and River Partners, to conduct ‘rabbit captures’ in the San Joaquin River National Wildlife Refuge in Modesto since August. Over the past three weeks, 20 captured rabbits were brought to Oakland Zoo’s veterinary hospital, where they received thorough physical exams and the RHDV2 vaccination. The rabbits are being closely monitored by Zoo veterinarians and staff to ensure that the vaccination has no adverse effects. Prior to this conservation effort, the RHDV2 vaccine has only been used on domestic rabbits, The current 20 rabbits serve as a safety trial for the use of the RHDV2 vaccine on wild populations. Monitoring of the rabbits at Oakland Zoo in the coming weeks will be key to predicting the success of more widespread vaccinations of this sub-species. “Conservation of species is very important to Oakland Zoo, both in captivity and in the wild. We, and all AZA-accredited zoos, play a unique role in conservation, in that we are able to use our extensive knowledge of animals and the care to also aid in saving those in the wild,” says Darren Minier, Assistant Director of Animal Care, Conservation & Research at Oakland Zoo. Following the monitoring period, if successful, the Riparian Brush rabbits will be returned to the wild at the San Joaquin River National Wildlife Refuge. Oakland Zoo will then help administer vaccinations to an additional 200 rabbits in the wild to protect them from the Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease Virus. Rabbits are an essential part of ecosystems as herbivores and as a primary food source to other animals. This program will help maintain their place in the ecosystem. Oakland Zoo continues in the practice of rescuing and rehabilitating animals for release back into the wild. For more information visit www.oaklandzoo.org/conservation-society-of-california.

articles.text: Like many other seasonal events across the Bay Area, this year’s Harvest Festival, originally scheduled for Piedmont Park on Sunday, September 27, will be a virtual celebration due to gathering restrictions brought on by the pandemic. “As disappointing as not having an in-person event is, the city recognizes that the most important thing right now is to keep the community safe and healthy,” said Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. “Because of the nature of the Harvest Festival, social distancing measures would not be possible to achieve, let alone enforce, during this event,” This year’s Festival will feature a photo contest and a youth coloring, drawing, and collage contest. The Recreation Department encourages Piedmont residents to share harvest gardening successes with the virtual festival. Residents and school district employees can email photos of their home-grown edibles, preserves and cooking at one photo per category. Photos may be sent directly to Putzer at cputzer@ piedmont.ca.gov. Submissions must include your name, category entered, email and home address. The deadline for photo submissions is Friday, September 18. Everyone who enters will get a participation ribbon and will be entered into a random drawing for a $60 gift certificate from Ace Grand Lake Nursery on October 5. Categories for submissions include: tomato, pumpkin, squash, jam, bread, mustard, best cookie, dried fruit and veggie, salsa, unusual fruit, curds and butters, jam, apple pie, cake, cucumber pickles, ugly edible, honey, preserved edible, “other” pie, pesto and sauce, preserved veggie, and compost pile. The youth coloring contest is sponsored by the Piedmont Garden Club. Kids ages 14 and younger can download a poster, create their own vegetable drawing or make a collage from the nature scavenger hunt page found on the recreation department’s website. E-mail a copy of the project to cputzer@piedmont.ca.gov. [This] is essentially a way to engage all the ages as we’re all sheltering in place,” said Susan Hill, founder of the Harvest Festival. She added that designing the festival virtually allows for a wider breadth of possibilities. For more infor mation, visit https://piedmont.ca.gov/ harvestfestival.

articles.text: Once again, the bicycle team Linda and Marvin will be riding in memory of Linda Lettieri and Marvin Stern, both of whom passed away from ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, better known as Lou Gehrig¹s Disease). July 9 marked the 13th anniversary of Linda¹s passing and the 15th year our bicycle team, Team Linda and Marvin, will be participating in the Ride to Defeat ALS. This is truly a science fiction-like disease in its progressive reduction of your ability to move, speak and eventually, breathe. Since ALS is currently not well understood, has no cure or effective treatment path, we are working hard to fund-raise to find a cure through the ALS Association, Golden West Chapter. Finally, there are some glimmers of hope that some of the genetics of ALS are being discovered, although we are a long way from effective treatments and the eventual cure. The ALS Association is the only non-profit organization fighting Lou Gehrig’s Disease on every front. By leading the way in global research, providing assistance for people with ALS through a nationwide network of chapters, coordinating multidisciplinary care through certified clinical care centers, and fostering government partnerships, The Association builds hope and enhances quality of life while aggressively searching for new treatments and a cure. Team Linda and Marvin will be riding Saturday, September 26 in their memory and we are soliciting your support to help our team exceed our fundraising goal for ALS research. Last year, through the amazingly generous donations of friends, family, and clients, we raised over $70,000 for ALS Research. The timeline for a cure or even a treatment for ALS may be very long, and we may not be around long enough to see it, but the goal is worthy of our effort and hopefully your dollars. Any contribution, no matter how small (or large!) will be appreciated and will help fund research into the causes and cures of ALS. Your tax-deductible gift will make a difference in the lives of many! It is faster and easier than ever to support this great cause. You can make your donation online by simply clicking on the link at the bottom of this message. If you would prefer, you can also send your tax-deductible contribution to the address listed below. Please write the name/Team Linda and Marvin in the memo line. Due to the Coronavirus, the ride is going virtual this year, but some of us will be riding from Oakland to the top of Mount Diablo and back, a distance of 80 miles and 7,500 feet of vertical climbing. That’s our challenge to support ALS research and care. We hope you will be compelled to support this cause in an effort to defeat this horrible disease. Thank you for your support. articles.text: The Piedmont Park Commission approved Autumn Blaze Maple trees as replacement of liquidambars on Bellevue Avenue. At the request of the residents at 60 Bellevue Avenue, the city’s Public Works staff met in December 2019 to review the street trees in front of their property. An outside arborist was called in to assess the condition of seven trees, three Liquidambar (Sweetgum) trees at 60 Bellevue, two Liquidambars at 64 Bellevue, and two Liquidambars and a Birch tree at 57 Bellevue. Kent recommended that city inspect adjacent trees if the streets, roadway, curb or gutter were to be repaired. If the roots can be pruned, then the trees could be saved. Across the street, at 47 Bellevue, a lone Liquidambar tree was approved for removal. The trees at 57 Bellevue are located “under high voltage lines,” Kent explained, which means they get severely pruned by PG&E. Because of that pruning, those trees have been recommended for removal. Residents at 60 Bellevue are currently planning a landscaping project, which is under review by the city Planning Commission. While all seven trees were assessed, Park Commissioners considered removing only three trees located at 60 Bellevue at the most recent Park Commission meeting, on September 2. “The applicant is requesting removal of these trees to accommodate the proposed construction, and proper replacement of the sidewalk, curb and gutter,” Kent said. One Liquidambar is causing substantial damage to the curb and roadbed, causing a depression, which is interrupting the drainage along Bellevue Avenue. It is expected that during the repair of the curb, substantial tree roots will be encountered from the mature Liquidambar. Following arborist recommendations, the root system needs to be exposed during demolition, and evaluation will be determined then if the tree can be preserved. Two species of trees were considered for the Bellevue block: Chinese Pistache and Autumn Blaze Maple. Both species are known to provide substantial shade and canopy, with impressive autumn colors. Chinese Pistache is a small to medium-sized tree, native to central and western China. The species is planted as a street tree in temperate areas worldwide due to its attractive fruit and autumn foliage. Autumn Blaze Maple, or Freeman maple, is a naturally occurring hybrid maple that is the result of a cross between Acer rubrum and Acer saccharinum. Wild specimens are found in eastern North America. Commissioner Jim Horner recommended the tree species Autumn Blaze Maple in place of Liquidambar, if the existing trees are to be removed. “The Liquidambar trees [on Bellevue] seem to have been doing well for a really long time. If the city is [trying] to gradually rotate out of Liquidambar to other species, the Autumn Blaze Maple is more consistent and would be a less dramatic change,” Horner said. Liquidambar tree branches can grow horizontal and vertical directions, which require considerable pruning. By Allyson Aleksey At the request of the residents at 60 Bellevue Avenue, the city’s Public Works staff met in December 2019 to review the street trees in front of their property. An outside arborist was called in to assess the condition of seven trees, three Liquidambar (Sweetgum) trees at 60 Bellevue, two Liquidambars at 64 Bellevue, and two Liquidambars and a Birch tree at 57 Bellevue. Kent recommended that city inspect adjacent trees if the streets, roadway, curb or gutter were to be repaired. If the roots can be pruned, then the trees could be saved. Across the street, at 47 Bellevue, a lone Liquidambar tree was approved for removal. The trees at 57 Bellevue are located “under high voltage lines,” Kent explained, which means they get severely pruned by PG&E. Because of that pruning, those trees have been recommended for removal. Residents at 60 Bellevue are currently planning a landscaping project, which is under review by the city Planning Commission. While all seven trees were assessed, Park Commissioners considered removing only three trees located at 60 Bellevue at the most recent Park Commission meeting, on September 2. “The applicant is requesting removal of these trees to accommodate the proposed construction, and proper replacement of the sidewalk, curb and gutter,” Kent said. One Liquidambar is causing substantial damage to the curb and roadbed, causing a depression, which is interrupting the drainage along Bellevue Avenue. It is expected that during the repair of the curb, substantial tree roots will be encountered from the mature Liquidambar. Following arborist recommendations, the root system needs to be exposed during demolition, and evaluation will be determined then if the tree can be preserved. Two species of trees were considered for the Bellevue block: Chinese Pistache and Autumn Blaze Maple. Both species are known to provide substantial shade and canopy, with impressive autumn colors. Chinese Pistache is a small to medium-sized tree, native to central and western China. The species is planted as a street tree in temperate areas worldwide due to its attractive fruit and autumn foliage. Autumn Blaze Maple, or Freeman maple, is a naturally occurring hybrid maple that is the result of a cross between Acer rubrum and Acer saccharinum. Wild specimens are found in eastern North America. Commissioner Jim Horner recommended the tree species Autumn Blaze Maple in place of Liquidambar, if the existing trees are to be removed. “The Liquidambar trees [on Bellevue] seem to have been doing well for a really long time.
